Denza Launching "God's Eye" Driving Assistance in Europe, the Z9GT Will Get It First
8 photos
Photo: Denza
The BYD-controlled Denza brand used the Mondial de l'Auto in Paris to announce "God's Eye" for Europe. Ominously named by certain accounts, the advanced driver assistance suite will be deployed in the Old Continent next year, starting with the flagship Z9GT shooting brake. City Navigation on Driving Assistance is what Denza calls the urban-centric level of God's Eye, and its functionalities will become available through an OTA update.
CNOA was programmed and tested in China to handle point-to-point navigation through city traffic, namely the environment where ordinary assistance systems fold up. The Z9GT for Europe will soon be able to stop at red lights on its own, yield at roundabout entries, obey posted speed limits automatically, and turn left across moving traffic at busy junctions.
City Navigation on Driving Assistance further times its way into and out of roundabouts through gaps in the flow, a maneuver that many beginner drivers obviously dread. The folks at Denza further boast lane changes around double-parked cars and slow traffic, cyclist and pedestrian detection while driving on narrow streets, and giving way to them.
Looking at the bigger picture, BYD is pitching Europe through Denza an easier commute. This system also comes with strings attached, the biggest one being that the driver must keep their eyes on the road to intervene whenever necessary. Beyond the software-only side of the system, the hardware is already there.
In the Z9GT , customers get 12 ultrasonic sensors, 11 cameras, three millimeter-wave radars, and one lidar setup. That's a whole lot of hardware, indeed, but having this many sensors and technologies working together seamlessly is the secret to preventing very problematic situations. Per UN regulation R171, systems in this class are allowed to support the driver with steering, acceleration, and braking as long as they're supervised.
Photo: Denza BYD and the Denza division have some coding to do before the urban-centric part of God's Eye becomes legal in the European Union. As of this writing, the software is claimed to be in an advanced stage of calibration and adaptation before seeking the R171-defined type approval required for Euro introduction. Driver's eye gaze and head posture monitoring have been confirmed, along with the position of their hands on the steering wheel.
Denza and the BYD group as a whole line up behind Tesla at this door. Having recently renamed the incredibly misleading Full Self-Driving suite to Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe, the American system has been cleared in a bunch of countries by the Dutch approval authority RDW. A UN working-party vote on Tesla Assisted Drive is due in December 2026 after a Belgian safety group published a damning report about Full Self-Driving on October 6.
Given how slow this gate can swing even for Tesla, the Denza brand's 2027 target should be viewed more as a plan rather than a promise. Chinese buyers, on the other hand, use God's Eye since 2025 in the urban jungle and on highways as well. The system's Euro-specific urban capability, therefore, is roughly two years behind China due to regulatory hurdles.
All in all, the Z9GT is the correct spearhead for such an ambitious ADAS. The grand tourer, which is available in purely electric and Super Hybrid DM-i flavors, is a tech-leaning luxury and sporty vehicle with a lot of muscle on tap. The electric version, for example, packs 850 kilowatts (1,140 mechanical horsepower). Opting for the 2.0-liter hybrid gets you 570 kW (764 hp) at full chatter.

AITO showed the AITO 9, AITO 8, AITO 7 and AITO 6 at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. Image: AITO
AITO will start selling cars in Europe in the fall of 2027. The Chinese luxury SUV brand, built by Seres with Huawei’s technology, confirmed the timing at the Paris Motor Show today, where it showed the AITO 9, 8, 7, and 6.
AITO sold 426,000 vehicles in 2025, more than any other Chinese luxury brand. Now it has a date for Europe. But you won’t find the word “Huawei” anywhere in its Paris press kit.
A year out, with a lot of paperwork left
AITO is giving itself 12 months, and it needs them. The brand says it’s still “actively pursuing” EU Whole Vehicle Type Approval, the certification any car needs to be sold in the bloc, and it’s targeting a five-star Euro NCAP rating under the 2026 protocol across its whole lineup.
Its briefing material also includes a pledge to comply with GDPR. That’s not something automakers usually feel the need to spell out, unless they expect European buyers to ask where their data goes.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The rest of the plan is localization: tuning the powertrains and chassis for European roads, multilingual voice controls in the cabin, adapting driver assistance and parking features “with partners,” and building a service network with local parts and customer support teams.
What’s missing is everything a buyer would care about. No prices. No launch markets. No dealer or distribution partners. No European specs.
And this isn’t the first time AITO has teased Europe. Seres showed the AITO 9, 8, and 5 at IAA Munich in September 2025 without giving any timeline. Seres has also been selling its own Seres 5 crossover in a couple of European markets, like Norway and Greece, for years.
Clifford Kang, Board Member and Vice President of SERES Group, announcing AITO’s plans to enter Europe in fall 2027. Image: AITO
“For AITO, New Luxury is where traditional luxury meets technological luxury,” said Clifford Kang, board member and vice president of Seres Group, during the press conference.
Big, fast, three-row SUVs
All four models are SUVs, and all of them are offered in China as both battery-electric and range-extended EVs (REEV), where a gas engine acts as a generator.
The flagship AITO 9 (sold as the M9 in China) is 5,285 mm long on a 3,125 mm wheelbase, putting it in BMW X7 and Mercedes GLS territory. AITO lists up to 497 kW (666 hp) and 0-100 km/h in 4.6 seconds, along with an 800V fully active suspension, rear-wheel steering, and a CATL battery. The five-seater is the EV version, while the six-seater uses the range extender.
At the other end, the AITO 6 is a 4,960 mm two-row SUV aimed at younger buyers. The EV version makes 340 kW and the REEV 345 kW, with 0-100 km/h in 5.2 seconds.
The company also names Bosch, CATL, Valeo, and Pirelli as suppliers, which is clearly meant to reassure European buyers.
The AITO 9 flagship SUV on display in Paris. The vehicles shown are China-spec models. Image: AITO
The Huawei-shaped hole
In China, AITO has been Huawei’s car brand in all but name. It was the first brand in Huawei’s Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance (HIMA). Huawei handled product definition, design, and sales through its own stores, and it supplied the driver-assistance system and HarmonyOS cockpit that sold the cars. Seres built them.
That arrangement wasn’t cheap. Seres reportedly paid Huawei roughly 10% per vehicle in licensing and channel fees, and its purchases from Huawei and its affiliates hit 56.05 billion yuan ($8.3 billion) in 2025.
It also just changed. On September 15, Seres took over AITO’s product definition, design, marketing, retail, and service, with Huawei moving to a support role. Two weeks later, the two companies signed a new five-year cooperation agreement.
So the Paris pitch credits the “SERES MF Platform” and unnamed “partners” instead. That makes sense for Europe, where several governments have restricted Huawei equipment in their 5G networks. AITO clearly wants buyers in Munich and Lyon to see a Seres brand, not a Huawei one.
Visitors and media at the AITO press conference at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. Image: AITO
Strong at home, but slowing
The track record in China is real. According to Seres’ annual results, AITO sold 426,000 vehicles in 2025, led by the AITO 8 (over 150,000), with the AITO 9 and AITO 7 above 110,000 each. The brand hit one million cumulative deliveries in 46 months.
But 2026 has been rougher. HIMA, where AITO is the biggest contributor, delivered 37,490 vehicles in September, down 29% year-over-year and its fourth straight monthly decline. Seres posted a 1.72 billion yuan net loss in the first half of 2026, compared with a 2.94 billion yuan profit a year earlier, as revenue fell 7.9%.
Then there’s trade policy. Chinese-built battery-electric cars face EU anti-subsidy tariffs of up to 35.3%, on top of the standard 10% import duty. Chinese automakers have leaned on plug-in hybrids to get around them , and AITO’s range-extended lineup would have fit right into that strategy.
That door is closing. On October 9, the EU and China agreed to halve Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid exports to the EU. Neither side has released the terms, so it’s not yet clear how range extenders will be treated.
AITO will also be late to the party. By fall 2027, it will be fighting BYD, which has already overtaken Tesla as the best-selling EV brand in key overseas markets , and Xpeng, which has been in talks to buy a Volkswagen plant in Europe , on top of the German luxury brands on their home turf.
Electrek’s Take
The AITO 9 is a genuinely impressive SUV, and Chinese buyers have spent real luxury money on it. On paper, the cabin tech and the performance match or beat what the German brands offer for the money.
The problem is that AITO’s success in China was built on Huawei. Huawei’s stores, Huawei’s software, Huawei’s brand recognition. Strip that out, and in Europe you have a big, fast, well-equipped SUV from a company almost nobody there has heard of, priced against BMW, Mercedes, and Volvo.
Chinese luxury brands have had a hard time in Europe so far. Nio has been at it for years with tiny volumes. Building a premium dealer and service network from scratch is slow and expensive, and AITO is doing it while its home sales are falling and Seres is losing money.
And the tariff picture keeps getting worse. The BEVs get hit with anti-subsidy duties, and the range-extender workaround is now being capped by an EU-China deal whose details we still don’t know.
A year out with no prices, no markets, and no partners, “autumn 2027” is a statement of intent, not a launch. We’ll take it seriously when there’s a price list and delivery dates.
If you’re shopping for a big electric SUV like the AITO 9, home solar is the cheapest way to fill that massive battery. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. One-Off Pagani Utopia Is a Striking Work of Art With 24K Gold and Actual Moon Dust
13 photos
Photo: Instagram/varryx
Throw together a passion for cars and the financial ability to spend millions to satisfy that passion, and you have the perfect recipe for a striking car collection with one-off units that wouldn't even exist otherwise. That is exactly how Kris Singh's garage got started.
Kris Singh is a famous hypercar collector millionaire that probably doesn't even need an introduction with car enthusiasts. He loves fast and unique cars just about as much as he loves a good pun and customization projects that he can get actively involved in, so the newest addition to his collection is a sum of all these things.
It's a Pagani Utopia with a unique and inimitable paintjob and an outrageous interior that strives to match it and do it justice. Singh calls it La Madonna of the Car Nation, an excellent pun on Leonardo's famous 15th century painting Madonna of the Carnation because this exact shade of gold that was used for the car is inspired by the one Leonardo used.
Singh took delivery of the vehicle just a few days ago, at the 2026 Pagani Raduno Vanishing Point event that took place in Sicily, Italy, and obviously turned the moment into a viral video. Noticeably proud and beyond ecstatic, he made sure to take his fans and followers along for the ride (heh!), giving them a glimpse at a vehicle that had been – quite literally – eight years in the making.
Photo: Instagram/sparky18888 It's not that painting the Utopia and customizing its interior took that long, but rather that Singh's idea took this long to take root. It first sprung to his mind in early 2018, when he bought a piece of rock from the Moon and he assumed that grinding it and using it as base for a custom paint would be the ultimate flex in car customization.
He wasn't wrong.
Later that year, Singh announced that he would be working with Karosserie to develop a custom paint called Karosserie Lunar Red, inspired by the iconic red sole of the Louboutin shoes and containing ground Lunar dust, for a new Aston Martin Valkyrie. By 2024, the plan fell through, seemingly because Aston Martin couldn't keep their end of the deal, or so Singh would end up saying on his social media.
Photo: Instagram/varryx Disappointed, he turned to Pagani, having already been a loyal customer for years. The paint that should have been used for the Valkyrie would go on a Utopia, and he would still become the first person to own a car painted with actual Moon dust.
Sometime down the road, the Karosserie Lunar Red became Karosserie Lunar Gold, as shown in the videos at the bottom of the page and the photos in the gallery. It's made with the ground Lunar rock and 24K gold bar shavings, and while it might look like a regular pearly/sparkly gold to the untrained eye, it's probably different if you can see it in person.
The interior matches the exterior in outrageousness, with black leather, gold stitching, and 24K gold covered elements throughout. It's more high fashion with a dash of divisiveness than space-inspired, leaning towards the opulence and maximalism of the House of Versace than the utilitarianism of space design or the classical beauty of the Leonardo painting.
Photo: Instagram/varryx Singh himself highlights the seven-speed gear shifter, the pedals, and the rims of the gauges on the dashboard, all of which are covered in 24K gold. The patterned gold and black leather seats are elaborate and vibrant, with a design that received input from Singh's partner, also shown in the video.
The 6.0-liter twin-turbo Mercedes- AMG V12 engine was put together and branded by Spark 18888 aka The King aka Rober Beit, a prominent hypercar collector and asset manager from Connecticut, and a good friend of Singh's. Millionaires always hang in tight circles, but hypercar collector millionaires even more so.
Of the 229 Pagani Utopias produced, only 99 are coupes, with one selling for about $2.5 million. Singh's is clearly much more valuable now, if only for its unique paintjob and the amount of gold used for customizing it. This much gold can't possibly be to everyone's tastes, but there's no denying the artistry and the hard work behind it.
Photo: Instagram/varryx The Madonna of the Car Nation joins a collection that includes a Pagani Huayra BC dubbed Macchina Volante, a Huayra La Monza Lisa, which happens to be the most driven Pagani in existence, a 1-of-5 Zonda Cinque, and a Veyron Grand Sport Vitesse formerly owned by Arnold Schwarzenegger.
Singh also owns several Bugattis, four Chirons, several Ferraris, Rolls-Royces, Lamborghinis, and Hummers .
Photo: Instagram/varryx Singh is said to be worth an estimated $200 million, so he clearly doesn't lack the funds to turn even his wildest dreams into (car) reality. Even if that takes eight long years, a public spat with Aston Martin, a piece of rock from the Moon, and whatever effort and money went into turning this Utopia into this sparkly, eye-catching piece of art. source_document.body:
French electric marine motor manufacturer TEMO is bringing its latest electric propulsion system to North America, offering sailboat owners an interesting middle ground between a conventional outboard and a permanently installed pod drive.
It’s been nearly two years since we last checked in on the French e-boat motor maker , but it appears they’ve used that time well to make several new advancements, chief among them the TEMO OUTPOD system.
The novel electric boat drivetrain will make its North American debut at the United States Sailboat Show in Annapolis, Maryland, later this week. The OUTPOD was previously awarded the Best Innovative Product prize at the 2025 Paris Nautic Show, and is now becoming available for boaters in the US .
There are several electric boat motors out there, and even a few specifically designed for sailboats. But the interesting part here is how TEMO has approached installation. Traditional pod drives generally require cutting into the boat’s hull, while electric outboards hang from the transom. The OUTPOD instead places an underwater pod drive on an external, bolt-on transom mount, meaning there’s no drilling below the waterline.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
The motor can also slide off its mount for storage or maintenance. A height-adjustable mast allows sailors to pull the entire motor out of the water using a halyard while sailing, eliminating the drag of leaving a propeller in the water. The shaft can rotate through 180 degrees for maneuvering and hydrogeneration.
TEMO is launching two versions. The OUTPOD 1000 produces 1,300 watts and 66 lb (30 kg) of static thrust, while the larger OUTPOD 3000 bumps that to 3,100 watts and 148 lb (67 kg) of thrust. Interestingly, the motor itself weighs just 26 lb (11.8 kg) in either version.
Power comes from removable 2.3 kWh batteries that slot into an auto-connecting rack, allowing owners to charge them either onboard using shore power or remove them for charging elsewhere. Sailors who already have a compatible 48V lithium battery bank can use that instead. It’s unclear if that only includes 48V batteries available from TEMO, but with so many commonly available large capacity 48V batteries these days , an open system could be quite convenient for sailors looking to add capacity or carry multiple batteries.
The system also supports both solar charging and hydrogeneration, allowing the propeller to feed energy back into the batteries while sailing.
It’s part of TEMO’s broader 48V SEASIDE ecosystem, which shares batteries and controls across several styles of electric marine motors ranging from 500W to 6kW.
The OUTPOD 1000 package starts at $2,600, while the OUTPOD·3000 carries a $5,400 MSRP. Both will be shown at the Annapolis show from October 15-18.
It’s another interesting example of how electrification can rethink marine propulsion rather than simply replacing a gasoline outboard with an electric one. For sailboats in particular, the ability to completely lift the drive out of the water when it isn’t needed – and then use it for hydrogeneration when desired – makes for a particularly compelling setup.

context_references.quote: Ban Keun will allow a “continuous” Chinese presence and primarily be used to “steer procurement to Chinese equipment” and support PLA air operations, the China Global South Project media platform says in a study.

source_document.body:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — China’s design to use a Laotian airport for joint military training has put much of Southeast Asia on guard about how far the People’s Liberation Army will extend its reach.
The China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport some 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the Lao capital Vientiane and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy kicked off in September, the Chinese Ministry of Defense said on its website.
China’s role at the military airport, which had just finished major upgrades and features a 2,000-meter runway, suggests that the People’s Liberation Army intends to springboard into other parts of Southeast Asia – a land-border neighbor where several countries have territorial differences with China – experts say.
“As China in reality aspires to be a major power, it has to gradually and in a low-key manner build up military bases, albeit for training or other seemingly innocuous purposes,” said Oh Ei Sun, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Center think tank in Kuala Lumpur.
“Laos has long been considered to be a close ally for (China) in Southeast Asia and it is of course no surprise that China’s first base in Southeast Asia is located there,” he added.
The two countries share a border, a Communist Party leadership and a recent history of economic cooperation led by large Chinese infrastructure projects such as a railway line.
The defense ministry in Beijing said the training center, to be jointly maintained and operated, is aimed at helping Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots.
Ban Keun will allow a “continuous” Chinese presence and primarily be used to “steer procurement to Chinese equipment” and support PLA air operations, the China Global South Project media platform says in a study.
The ministry website says China’s role at the airport is “not directed against any third party”, contributing instead to improving “practical military cooperation.”
But instead, China may be increasing its military foothold “deep inside mainland Southeast Asia” after earlier establishing a naval presence at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base, said Nguyen Thanh Trung, a political scientist at Fulbright University in Vietnam. Mainland Southeast Asia includes Vietnam, Malaysia, Myanmar and Thailand as well as Laos and Cambodia.
Chinese operational military presence and privileged access at the Cambodian base grew from 2019 through 2025, Asian mainstream media reports have said.
China is keen on Laos now “because the Chinese feel it’s time to complement the naval facility in Cambodia with nearby air power capability,” said Denny Roy, a ­senior fellow at the East-West Centre think tank in Hawaii.
Using both its navy and air force, Beijing has shored up its South China Sea claims over the past two decades by building artificial islands, often for military use. Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam dispute parts of the sea with China.
Sporadic China-Vietnam incidents have occurred in the waters since the 1970s. China and the Philippines are jousting for control over tiny islets west of Luzon and Palawan islands.
“Vietnam is probably the most sensitive, as Laos has long been its strategic buffer, and for now the foothold looks more like China asserting leverage over Hanoi and Phnom Penh,” said Hangyu Lee, East Asia Pacific analyst at the nonprofit organization Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project. He said Ban Keun and Ream “together could look like a wider Chinese security network.”
Myanmar, Lee added, could be “indirectly affected” if the airport improves China’s ability to monitor activity across continental Southeast Asia. Myanmar, with its own Chinese border, has been in civil war since 2021.
China’s presence at the Laotian airport has been linked to its first confirmed overseas base, in the East African country Djibouti. The People’s Liberation Army uses it as a support base. The African base and now Ban Keun mark China’s gradual, low-key buildup of bases, Oh said.
But the Laotian site “represents a new air-centered model” distinct from Djibouti and Ream in Cambodia, the China Global South Project study says.
“Eventually it can be a pre-positioned base for PRC aircraft as needed ,” Roy said. “It could also be expanded to accommodate more and larger aircraft.”

Many transportation executives seem to place vehicle compliance in the same mental category as expense reports and badge renewals. It’s necessary, but it’s largely forgettable and delegated to the back office. That might have made sense when fleets were smaller and simpler, but it breaks down as soon as a fleet crosses state lines, adds vehicles faster than it adds people, or absorbs another company’s assets through acquisition.
Registrations, titles, taxes, permits, credentials, filings, and renewals aren’t paperwork about the fleet. They’re the legal condition the fleet operates under. A truck that’s fueled, inspected, and road-ready but sitting on an expired registration isn’t a viable fleet asset for a customer waiting on a load. It’s unavailable for an inexcusable reason.
Scale and geography multiply the complexity of vehicle compliance in ways that are easy to underestimate. Every additional state brings its own agency, its own deadlines, its own exceptions, and its own system quirks. A fleet that operates in five states is managing five sets of rules that rarely line up; a fleet that operates in thirty is managing a level of administrative complexity that requires a lot more than simple back-office delegation.
“Leading fleets are not focused on compliance alone; they are focused on operational continuity,” said Stephanie Schmidt, Vice President of Client Service at J. J. Keller & Associates, Inc . “Expert-led vehicle compliance can reduce administrative burden, improve visibility into fleet assets, and help ensure critical compliance activities are executed consistently. As an example, outsourcing vehicle compliance allows internal teams to stay focused on customers, growth, and day-to-day operations rather than managing complex regulatory processes.”
Executives often underestimate how directly administrative compliance affects asset availability. A vehicle that is mechanically ready but administratively unable to operate is still an unavailable asset, turning what appears to be a paperwork issue into an operational and financial one.
Compliance work absorbs more than clerical hours. It requires staff who understand deadline cadences across jurisdictions, who can validate data against agency requirements, who know how to chase down an agency that’s slow to respond, and who can handle the exceptions that don’t fit the standard process. That expertise takes years to build, and once it’s built, it’s rarely replaceable on short notice.
The real cost shows up as opportunity cost. Every hour an experienced operations or safety employee spends untangling a title problem or a registration exception is an hour not spent on customers, growth initiatives, or operational priorities. Executives are left with a narrower set of choices than they’d like: add headcount, pull people off higher-value work, accept slower turnaround on renewals and filings, or absorb more risk.
“Vehicle compliance extends well beyond renewals and registrations,” Schmidt said. “Each jurisdiction has its own requirements, timelines, processes, and regulatory nuances, making experienced professionals and established agency relationships difficult to replace. As organizations face turnover or staffing changes, having consistent access to dedicated specialists helps preserve consistency, reduce risk, and keep fleets operating legally and efficiently.”
For growing fleets, the question is less whether compliance work gets done and more whether the organization has a sustainable model for executing it at scale.
The fleets most exposed to compliance risk are often the ones that are otherwise performing well. They’re growing quickly, adding lanes, or expanding into new states. An inefficient process that worked cleanly when the fleet had a few hundred units and operated in a handful of states can show weak points at a few thousand units across dozens of jurisdictions. More vehicles mean more transactions, more renewal cycles, more exceptions, and more agency systems to navigate, each with its own quirks and requirements.
Growth by acquisition compounds the problem. Research from the J. J. Keller Center for Market Insights found that 94% of transportation organizations encountered unexpected risks or complexities during a merger or acquisition, with documentation and recordkeeping among the most common challenges. An additional 93% reported significant concerns during the transaction process, including operational disruption and delays. Vehicle compliance often sits at the center of those risks because acquired assets must be integrated into existing compliance processes without interrupting operations.
“One of the less visible challenges of an acquisition is ensuring every acquired asset can continue operating legally and without interruption,” Schmidt said. “Vehicle compliance becomes a business continuity issue when fleets inherit different registration practices, title-management processes, and state requirements. Experienced partners and proven processes can help protect operational continuity during periods of rapid growth and change.”
Institutional knowledge is one of the hardest things to scale. The person who knows why a particular state handles a filing differently, or which agency contact to call when a renewal stalls, is difficult to replace, and nearly impossible to replicate quickly when a fleet doubles in size or absorbs a new set of jurisdictions overnight.
The consequences of a compliance breakdown rarely stay contained to the back office. A missed renewal can delay dispatch on a load that’s already been sold. An incomplete filing can turn into an urgent, all-hands correction. An expired credential can create exposure at a roadside inspection that costs far more in downtime and driver disruption than the filing itself would have. None of these show up on a compliance dashboard until they’ve already become an operations problem like downtime, rework, lost productivity, customer complaints, and lost time and revenue associated with each.
The cost of noncompliance includes the cost of interruption, and those costs can compound in unpredictable ways. A delayed load, for instance, can cost a customer relationship or reputation.
Disaster preparedness is a subset of this same risk, especially as it pertains to proper storage and handling of documentation.
“Vehicle titles are among the most critical documents tied to a fleet, yet many organizations store them across multiple offices, filing systems, or locations,” Schmidt said. “Secure offsite title management helps protect these assets from loss, damage, theft, or natural disaster while keeping records accessible when needed. As part of a broader risk-management strategy, it gives leaders confidence that ownership documentation remains protected during unforeseen events.”
None of this means every fleet should outsource compliance. It means every fleet should evaluate whether its current approach can reliably support growth, turnover, and increasing regulatory complexity.
An internal model works when an organization can sustain the specialization, staffing depth, and backup coverage that multi-jurisdiction compliance demands. A hybrid model keeps core ownership in-house while routing high-volume, specialized, or exception-heavy work to outside support. A fully externally supported model makes sense when predictable execution, geographic reach, or scalable capacity are difficult to maintain internally, especially through growth or turnover.
The goal in any of these arrangements should be to strengthen execution wherever the organization’s internal model is stretched thin.
Executives should be asking these questions: Does current staffing have the capacity to absorb deadlines, exceptions, and growth? Is the team’s jurisdictional expertise deep enough to survive turnover? What level of risk is acceptable when work is delayed or done incorrectly? How exposed is asset availability to an administrative failure? Can the current model scale as the fleet’s footprint changes? And where should internal expertise be concentrated for the greatest return to the business?
Vehicle compliance is no longer a back-office function for complex, multi-state fleets. It is a business capability that directly influences fleet readiness, growth, and risk. The strongest operating model is the one that gives leaders confidence that vehicles can remain legally available to serve customers as the business evolves.

source_document.body:
The flagship seven-seater is BYD’s first vehicle in Europe to feature its second-generation batteries and Flash Charging tech, delivering over 400 miles of range.
BYD launches new flagship Atto 8 in Europe
“BYD is all about turning intelligence into reality,” Stella Li, the company’s executive vice president, said on Monday.
The Atto 8 is the “perfect example,” Li added, featuring its latest breakthrough tech, including its second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging system.
Introduced at the Paris Auto Show, the flagship SUV is the first BYD vehicle to feature its Flash Charging system, enabling it to recharge just as fast as filling up at the gas station. It takes just five minutes to charge from 10% to 80%.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
A full recharge, or going from 10% to 97%, takes just nine minutes. According to BYD, that’s about a third of the time rival SUVs take to go from 10% to 80%.
Even in temperatures as low as -30°C, it requires only 12 minutes for the vehicle’s battery to recharge from 20% to 97%.
BYD Atto 8 at a Flash Charging station (Source: BYD)
Measuring 5,040 mm long, 1,996 mm wide, and 1,760 mm tall, the Atto 8 is about the size of other full-size electric SUVs, such as the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9.
BYD’s flagship SUV comes in two all-electric variants with the choice of rear- and all-wheel-drive powertrains.
The Design RWD model has a single rear motor producing 456 hp (340 kW) and 269 lb-ft (365 Nm) of torque, which BYD said delivers a 0 to 62 mph time of eight seconds.
BYD Atto 8 (Source: BYD)
Powered by a 115 kWh BYD Blade 2.0 battery, the Atto 8 offers an impressive WLTP range of up to 405 miles (600+ km). For example, BYD said the flagship SUV offers enough electric range to drive from London to Edinburgh.
The Atto 8 Excellence AWD, on the other hand, adds a front electric motor for a combined output of 764 hp (570 kW) and 572 lb-ft (775 Nm) of torque. The added power delivers a sports-car-rivaling 0- 62 mph acceleration time of 4.6 seconds and a WLTP range of 374 miles.
BYD Atto 8 interior (Source: BYD)
Inside, natural light fills the spacious cabin thanks to a 2.39m2 panoramic glass roof. Both Atto 8 variants have a 10.25″ digital instrument cluster, a 26″ head-up display, and a 15.6″ central infotainment touchscreen with Google Built-in.
BYD said the Atto 8 is specifically tailored for those looking for a “zero compromise” seven-seat SUV.
The front seats and outer seats of the middle row feature heating, ventilation, and massage functions. Rear passengers get their own air-conditioning control panel. All seats are upholstered in genuine leather.
The Design RWD model features a 10-speaker sound system, while the Excellence AWD gains a 21-speaker DiSound audio system, plus an added front refrigerator.
With the second and third rows folded, the Atto 8 offers up to 1,960L capacity. Even with all three rows up, the full-size SUV offers 270L of luggage space. Plus, there’s a 136L frunk (front trunk).
BYD said dealers in Europe will begin selling the Atto 8 in the first quarter of 2027. Prices have yet to be announced, but given it will be positioned above the Ti 7 , a plug-in hybrid seven-seat SUV, it will likely start at slightly over £47,995 ($65,000) on the road in the UK.
In Europe, BYD currently sells the Tang, an electric seven-seat SUV. In Germany, the BYD Tang typically starts at €75,000 ($84,000), but it’s currently on sale for €47,990 ($54,000).

Hyundai Tucson N Line Steals the Spotlight in Paris, but It's All Show and No Go
18 photos
Photo: Hyundai
Hyundai has just unveiled the all-new Tucson N Line at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. While it is definitely a showstopper, taking the bold "Art of Steel" design language to a whole new and sportier level, don't expect any power upgrade from Hyundai's latest crossover.
Hyundai's all-new Tucson lineup receives the N Line variant with a look that screams performance. It looks much sportier than its standard sibling, featuring aggressive track-inspired elements, which place it at the top of the Tucson range. Bigger wheels and mild suspension adjustments are also on the menu.
The crossover retains the standard proportions, which means it is 185.0 inches (4,700 millimeters) long, 75.0 inches (1,905 millimeters) in width, 66.3 inches (1,685 millimeters) tall, and sits on a wheelbase of 109.6 inches (2,785 millimeters). Those are the proportions for the North American and Asian markets, as the crossover sold in Europe is 178.5 inches (4,560 millimeters) long, with a wheelbase of 107.1 inches (2,720 millimeters).
The N Line is designed to mimic the looks of a sports car. It comes with a much larger and angular bumper, a dark chrome Parametric Jewel Hidden Lights grille, along with a pronounced chin spoiler and aero ducts at the edges finished in distinct satin black.
Photo: Hyundai The side profile integrates slimmer fender claddings, matching side skirts, and gloss-black side mirrors. It rides on model-specific 19- or 20-inch alloy wheels with premium grippy tires. The rear end gets the full-width LED light bar, body-coloured diffuser-effect inserts, and a twin-tip exhaust with sporty brightwork.
The cabin focuses on a darker, track-oriented theme, with no compromise on space, comfort, or practicality. This Black Monotone theme integrates part-suede and leather sport seats with contrasting red stitching, bright metal pedal covers, metal footrests, and branded kick plates. The driver controls the steering via the N steering wheel with perforated leather hand grips.
The Tucson N Line retains the 9.9-inch digital instrument cluster, paired with either the 12.9-inch or the larger 17.0-inch central touchscreen. Dual 15W wireless charging pads and heavy-duty 100W USB-C ports are also part of the plan, while an optional 12-speaker Bang & Olufsen sound system provides the soundtrack in the cabin.
The all-new Hyundai Tucson N Line uses the exact same engines as its siblings. It is just a trim with no extra oomph. However, the development of a high-performance Tucson N has officially been confirmed. The future model is expected to completely ditch fuel-sipping logic to focus entirely on speed and performance.
Photo: Hyundai In the meantime, the N Line can be ordered with any of the three distinct powertrains, from the base 1.6-liter four-cylinder turbo engine with 148 horsepower (150 metric horsepower) and front-wheel drive to the range-topping plug-in hybrid with 284 horsepower (288 metric horsepower) and all-wheel drive.
Hyundai hasn't released any pricing details for the new Tucson , not to mention the new Tucson N Line, but you shouldn't expect anything under $40,000 for the latter. The automaker also brought the new Bayon to Paris.

US Navy explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) technicians assigned to Explosive Ordnance Disposal Mobile Unit (EODMU) 2 and Peruvian Navy EOD technicians assigned to Peruvian Special Operations conduct limpet mine training utilizing the VideoRay Mission Specialist Defender while participating in UNITAS 2026, a US Naval Forces Southern Command and US Fourth Fleet-sponsored training exercise at Callao Naval Base, Peru, Sept. 14, 2026. (US Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Jackson Adkins.)
Maritime mines are a concern for the US and its allies in a number of regions, including the Strait of Hormuz and the South China Sea. In addition to being a threat to military vessels, mines can slow or halt commercial traffic through important trade and oil routes.
Breaking Defense spoke with Bryan Clark, director of the Hudson Institute’s Center for Defense Concepts and Technology, on the threat of mines, how they can be neutralized and the role of remote mine hunting in keeping personnel out of harm’s way.
Breaking Defense: Why are maritime mines such a serious threat in some of these strategic choke points like the Strait of Hormuz or the South China Sea?
Clark: Partly because they’re so easy to obtain or build, and then deploy. The Iranians even have rockets that can deploy mines at a standoff distance into the strait. That’s just an example of how easy it is to put these mines out there because you don’t need to precision guide them. You just drop them into the approximate area of the channel and that’s going to be sufficient to hold up traffic.
Mines don’t have to be sophisticated. There are obviously very sophisticated ones that look for particular acoustic or magnetic signatures. There are some that’ll measure how many ships go across and detonate on the third or fourth ship, but they don’t need to be smart in order to be effective. All you need is somebody to detect the mine and know that it’s there, and it’s going to cause vessel traffic to stop until the mine threat has been eliminated.
The barrier to entry is low. Countries can easily field a capable mine-laying capability or mine-laying force and then deny access in a critical strait or choke point. You have countries out there for whom mines are the main weapon, like Finland. When they think about having to face off against the Russians, the first thing they plan on doing is mining the Gulf of Finland, which prevents access to and from Sevastopol or St. Petersburg. You’ve cut off one of Russia’s only warm water ports by closing off the Gulf of Finland, and that’s for them their primary offensive capability.
For Iran, obviously the drone revolution has given them another offensive weapon, but mines have always been one of their main go-tos in terms of offensive weapons. It’s always been perceived that they would try to use them to close off the Strait of Hormuz because it is such a narrow choke point and so vital to global commerce.
The other thing about mines that makes them more potent as a threat is that you’d only need the threat of a mine in order to close off access. If you have a mine detection or even a concern about mines, vessel traffic will generally stop until the threat’s been verified or validated, or shipping companies decide to accept the risk and either pay higher insurance rates or accept the potential loss of their own ship. It’ll impact shipping even if you just have the threat of a mine without the physical presence of them. That makes them an effective tool even for small countries.
US Navy explosive ordnance disposal (EOD) technicians assigned to Explosive Ordnance Disposal Mobile Unit (EODMU) 2 and Peruvian Navy EOD technicians assigned to Peruvian Special Operations conduct mine countermeasure operations while participating in UNITAS 2026, a US Naval Forces Southern Command and US Fourth Fleet-sponsored training exercise, El Paraiso, Peru, Sept. 19, 2026. (U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Jackson Adkins.)
How do you determine if a mine is a valid threat?
You can’t discount the threat. Because shipping companies don’t want to accept the risk of them being wrong or you being wrong if you say, ‘there’s not really a mine threat’ You have to take it at face value.
The first thing you do is find a channel that’s mine-free. That’s what the US did early on in the war. They used the remote-mine hunting systems they had to verify that the channel along the Omani coast was free of mines. Once you’ve verified a channel free of mines, it doesn’t necessarily matter that there might be mines elsewhere. You can lead ships through that safe passage, and then if you want to increase traffic or provide for more two-way traffic, then you have to expand the channel and search a larger area.
How does the Navy currently hunt and neutralize mines, and how has that task become less dangerous?
It used to be very dangerous, because you’d have to send a human-operated minesweeper out, which puts people at risk. Mine-hunting ships have been traditionally wooden or fiberglass to avoid creating a magnetic signature. They use a sonar system on the front to detect the mines and then they will have a sweep system they tow on the back or they’ll use neutralization systems to neutralize the mines after they find them.
Now the systems they use are robots. They have active sonars on board that they use to search for mines. It becomes kind of like a Roomba, where the robots go up and down the route looking for mines in the water column. They’ll stay near the surface and then look down into the water, and as long as the water is not extremely deep, they’ll be able to see the first 100 or 200 feet of water and detect mine-like objects.
They’ll identify things that they think are mines. When they do their run and come back, you download all the data off of them into a computer, which has processing software that helps you to figure out what are things that need further investigation.
Then you can send out another set of robots to investigate the things that might be mines to get a better idea of whether they’re really mines or if they were objects dumped on the seafloor or, things floating in the water that aren’t mines. That usually narrows down how many things you have to investigate further.
At the point you’ve determined there’s mine or mine-like objects in the water that have to be neutralized, you then send out a helicopter or a small boat with a mine neutralization system on it, which is a floating vehicle that has little torpedoes that’ll come off of it and those are fiber-optically guided to the target. You have a video screen and a joystick, and you steer those mine neutralizers to the mine and they detonate on that object.
Either they blow up the mine – if it’s a mine – or they punch a hole in it and it sinks to the bottom. These mine neutralizers have been around for 20 years or so, but they do keep the people out of the minefield.
It keeps people out of the minefield because now you don’t have to have the minesweeper driving into the minefield anymore. You can also do it at a greater scale. Because I can buy a lot more robots than I can buy minesweepers, because every minesweeper needs a crew and people are expensive. If you want to expand your mine-hunting fleet, you end up having to buy a bunch of manned ships. If you’re buying robots instead, you can buy a bunch of robots, store them, and then bring them out when you need to do the mine-hunting operation.
As you look forward, what do you see as the capabilities that will be needed most for counter-mine operations?
Onboard processing and communications. One of the limitations of the current way of doing it is you have to have the vessels or the vehicles doing the mine hunting come back and download all their data, then analyze it and then send out another set of vehicles to go investigate the likely mine areas to verify, and then send out another set of vehicles to go do the mine neutralization – helicopters and small boats with mine-neutralization systems. It’s a multi-pass setup the way it is now.
If instead you had onboard processing from these mine-hunting vehicles, the underwater vehicles looking for the mines could come up and transmit data back to you immediately and say, ‘I finished path one. I found a bunch of mines or potential mines. They’re here.’ Then you can quickly decide whether to send another vehicle out there right now to investigate, or to just send the mine neutralization system out immediately.
You should be able to get to a point where you can do this in a way that is just robot after robot after robot.

2027 Hyundai Bayon Finally Looks More Like a Box and Less Like an Egg
12 photos
Photo: Hyundai
Confirming the rumors that have been floating for a while now, South Korean carmaker Hyundai pulled the wraps off the newest version of the Bayon SUV at the 2026 Paris Motor Show that opened its doors this week. Technically a new generation of the compact SUV , it kind of feels more like a facelift to the facelift of two years ago.
Sure, Hyundai did give this model a fresh look by adopting a more angular interpretation of the Art of Steel design philosophy that governs its present-day models, and a fresh lineup of engines, but it’s not exactly a complete redesign. In fact, Hyundai itself doesn’t call this Bayon the second generation, but something that is more than an update.
The first thing worth mentioning is that the vehicle now rides on a longer wheelbase in a bid to allow for more legroom, especially at the rear. Standing at 2,600 mm, the new underpinnings support a body that measures 2,245 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and at most 1,565 mm high with roof rails.
The South Koreans don’t go into the specifics of just how much legroom there is now in the back, but we are told it’s more than before. Also, the passengers in the back are now treated to reclining, heated seats, a center armrest, and air ducts dedicated to them.
Photo: Hyundai Since many of the upgrades performed on the new Bayon target the SUV’s interior, I’ll go on by telling you that there is now a set of 12.3-inch curved displays (infotainment and instrument cluster) at the front, and that smartphones can now be connected wirelessly to the car, as well as to the Apple CarPlay and Android Auto solutions.
In a bid to make things feel a bit more premium, Hyundai installed a Bose sound system with eight speakers inside, and an openable panoramic sunroof for those who want it. Front ventilated and heated seats are also part of the deal.
For the exterior, the changes made compared to the previous generation manifest themselves in the form of sharper lines, finally making the SUV look more like a box than an egg, something I personally prefer to see.
There will probably be several trim levels on the market for the European buyers the SUV is meant for, but the highlight of the lineup is the N Line. As usual, this version comes with a touch of extras all around, right from the factory floor, starting with the 18-inch wheels that make the connection to the ground to the black roof.
Photo: Hyundai The same N Line has been imagined with dedicated lower-bumper winglets, a diffuser at the rear which integrates twin exhaust outlets, and cloth and textile suede seats inside the cabin.
When it comes to the heart of the new f , Hyundai will rely at first on two internal combustion engines, both displacing one liter, but delivering distinct power levels. One is rated at up to 80 hp, while the other at 113 hp. Both can be fitted with either a six-speed manual transmission or a seven-speed DCT.
The king of the Bayon engine lineup comes a little later in 2027 in the form of the 1.6 HEV 6DCT. As the name implies, this one brings together the benefits of a 1.6-litre GDI engine with those of an electric motor and a six-speed dual-clutch transmission.
The combined output of the system is rated at 136 hp and 265 Nm of torque, making this version the top-of-the-line model from as soon as it hits the market. Being a hybrid of this kind also means the Bayon will make use of adaptive regenerative braking and steering-wheel paddle shifters that will allow drivers to manually select the regeneration level.
Photo: Hyundai It’s not exactly clear when the all-new Hyundai Bayon will hit the market, or how much it will cost. For reference, the current version sells on the European market for prices that start at around 16,000 euros, which is the equivalent of around $18,000 at today’s exchange rates.
It’s likely the South Korean carmaker will try to keep pricing low, despite the fact that there are plenty of changes thrown into the mix compared to the present-day version. It’s unlikely, though, that many Europeans will go for the butt-naked version.
To make sure of that, Hyundai is throwing in a lot of optional extras, starting from the choice of wheels (up to 18 inches) to three distinct matte finishes that make the Bayon the only model in its segment to display matte colors.
There will be no Bayon version for the American market. For the Old Continent, the model will be assembled in Turkey, where Hyundai operates a major facility. We will keep an eye on things and come back to this story once we learn more about the starting prices for the SUV, as well as the market availability of the hybrid powertrain.

1970s Winnebago Brave RV Gets Hellcat Engine, Becomes 700-Horsepower Hemibago
10 photos
Photo: Tommy Boshers/YouTube
I've seen quite a few vintage Winnebago RVs saved from junkyards over the years. Many rescuers said they will fix them and put them back on the road, usually with a modern engine. And every single time I thought that it would be cool if someone stuck a Hellcat V8 between the seats. Well, it finally happened!
A few years ago, a guy named Tommy Boshers found an old Winnebago Brave that had been sitting for a while. The RV became a father-and-son type of project involving Chrysler's mean Hellcat powerplant. The camper is finally up and running. It's also doing burnouts, because what are you going to do with 700 horsepower anyway, right?
This isn't your typical restomod, though. While custom rigs are usually modified beyond their stock appearance, this Winnebago still looks very familiar. Tommy kept mods to a minimum but did just enough to make it stand out. The side panels are green, and the iconic W in the side stripes was replaced with H (for Hellcat). There's a big "Hemibago" logo on the roof and Hellcat emblems just below the side windows.
The interior is still as old-school as they get. I can't confirm everything is still original, but it sure looks like this Winnebago soldiered on without notable alterations as far as interior amenities go. And I think that's pretty cool. On the flipside, it seems that old cupboards and powerful engines don't go well together; Tommy had to use duct tape to prevent them from opening when the pedal hits the metal.
As for the Hellcat mill, it's most likely a crate engine. Mopar has been offering various iterations of the powerplant for years now. The standard Hellcat may not be available right now, but Chrysler is still offering the Redeye variant.
The supercharged 6.2-liter V8 debuted for the 2015 model year in SRT versions of the Dodge Challenger and Charger. It also found its way into the Jeep Grand Cherokee in 2018 and the Dodge Durango in 2021. Ram also offered a Hellcat-powered iteration of the 1500 pickup truck, which is still in production as of 2026. The Challenger Demon is also powered by a beefed-up Hellcat unit.
Depending on the car and the specs, the Hellcat delivered between 707 and 1,025 horsepower over the years. Tommy describes the Winnebago as a 700-horsepower RV but doesn't mention whether he dynoed the mill or not. But needless to say, this Winnebago is awfully fast for an old RV.
Of course, dropping a Hellcat in a big, boxy camper is not as easy as it sounds. Tommy struggled to fit the massive V8 between the front seats and needed bigger brakes to bring the RV to a halt safely. Unsurprisingly, the engine destroyed the driveshaft soon after the first burnout session.
I'm sure he still has a few gremlins to take care of, but this Winnebago is one heck of a rig. Much more so for me since I'm also a fan of the Brave.
The original Brave was a class A RV. It was introduced in 1970, a few years after Winnebago literally revolutionized the RV market with affordable campers using their thermo-panel sidewall construction. The Brave was also the first to use the company's "flying W" logo on the sidewalls.
The RV was built on a Dodge M300 commercial truck chassis and featured various Chrysler V8 engines. The Brave remained in production mostly unchanged through the 1980s, and it's now a desirable classic.

source_document.body:
The South Carolina-based startup Powerus unveiled a fully autonomous version of its Guardian interceptor on Monday at the Association of the United States Army ’s annual meeting.
Brett Velicovich, the company’s president and co-founder, said in an interview with Military Times that logical product upgrades have been key to the company’s success. He explained how the company’s growth, the evolution of its interceptors and rising U.S. military demand for drone-defense systems amid the war in Iran have converged.
“You know, the U.S. government had a big problem at the beginning of the Iran war, when they sent a bunch of Ukrainian interceptors to the Middle East thinking that it was going to solve a problem,” he said.
According to analysis by the Congressional Budget Office, the U.S. used roughly two-thirds of its inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors by Aug. 1 to stop drones like Iran’s Shahed. Because rebuilding the supply could take years and cost billions, the government has sought quicker and cheaper solutions like those used in Ukraine, but implementing them hasn’t been easy.
“When you go to Ukraine, most of the interceptors, believe it or not, are manually controlled,” he said, explaining that Ukrainian operators are highly skilled at finding and stopping one-way attack drones in the air. “And that’s great for Ukraine, where you could probably throw a rock and hit a drone pilot.”
The problem with the government’s initial thinking, according to Velicovich, was that Ukraine has a “proper drone army,” as the country has “entire brigades that are pilots. So those guys have extreme combat experience in knowing how to take a drone and send it into another drone. In other countries, they don’t.”
With that understanding, Velicovich explained how Powerus provided the U.S. with the Guardian 1 — modeled after manually controlled Ukrainian drone interceptors — to the semi-autonomous Guardian 2, which, when paired with a radar to detect threats, will launch the interceptor in the direction of a drone.
“It’ll know the speed and the telemetry. It’ll launch it in that direction, but you still have to do that final phase of manual kill,” he said.
And finally, Powerus developed the fully autonomous Guardian 3. He explained that when the radar cues it, the system launches in the direction of the threat and can detect and strike using artificial intelligence and navigation systems.
“So you kind of take the human error out of it,” he said.
Velicovich credits this strategy, which he and his team derived from first-hand experience in the military and using drones in combat, to the company’s recent success.
In about one year, Powerus has transformed into a publicly traded company with a market capitalization of nearly $390 million. On Oct. 1, it completed a merger with Aureus Greenway Holdings Inc., a golf course holding company backed by the two eldest Trump sons .
As the U.S. government looks for ways to find low-cost drone interceptors, it’s also looking for low-cost missile interceptors. Power has partnered with the Netherlands-based defense company Destinus to help meet that challenge.
“Destinus brings this just overwhelming, incredible ownership of the technology,” Velicovich said, adding that Powerus will be its “business development channel in the U.S. to sell systems that otherwise had not really been sold here yet.”
He added that Powerus received the demand signal from the Pentagon and aims to deliver.
“We know you’d be crazy not to buy these products because of just how effective they are on the battlefield,” he said.
About Daniel Terrill
Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.
